Tidylio
Your Laundry Voice Assistant
Team
Angela Molina (Case Study Author)  ·  May Kim  ·  Manvi Shah  ·  Vasilios Nikolopoulos
Professor
Sai Shruthi Chivukula

We wanted to design a laundry assistant that felt like it belonged in the room, not like a new gadget you had to learn. The challenge was figuring out how to give it a body.

The Problem
Laundry is easy to forget about

Laundry takes a long time but does not require your full attention, which means it is easy to forget about mid-cycle. You start a wash, go do something else, and an hour later your clothes are sitting wet in the machine. Timers help, but they just add another notification to ignore.

We wanted something that could track the process and check in at the right moments, without needing a screen or demanding constant attention. The idea was to design a voice assistant that lives in the laundry space, connected to your washer and dryer via Bluetooth, and aware of what is happening without you having to tell it.

Exploring the Form
We tried three different objects first

The first question was what the assistant should look like. The idea was to use a physical object that already belongs in a laundry room and let that object communicate through movement rather than speech, sound, or light alone.

We sketched out three options and mapped each one to the same set of states: standby, listening, processing, acting, reporting, and failure.

Soap bubble
Light and reactive. States communicated through expanding, floating, and popping.
Laundry pod
Internal movement. States shown through swirling and energy building inside the pod.
Fabric basket
Structural and flexible. States communicated through stretching, squishing, and shifting form.

All three worked as concepts, but they felt very different in practice. The bubble was hard to read as a reliable assistant because bubbles pop and float away making it difficult to come back to its standby mode. The pod was interesting but because of its material it did not allow much movement or differences between states without external objects. Which brought us to the the basket making the most sense on multiple levels.

The basket is already in the room. It does not need to explain itself.

It is directly tied to the laundry context, it has enough physical range to show different states clearly, and it feels stable rather than fragile. Since it is made of fabric, it can stretch, twist, compress, and collapse in ways that still look believable. We went with a cylindrical linen-type basket specifically because the simple shape made the movement easier to read.

Naming and Personality
Giving it a character

We spent time on the name because it shapes how the assistant feels to interact with. We tried combinations of laundry-related words and softer, name-like endings and landed on Tidylio, a mix of "tide" and "-elio." It sounds like a name without being too cute or too corporate.

The personality we aimed for was warm and helpful without being chatty. Tidylio is the kind of assistant that reminds you before you forget rather than alerts you after something goes wrong. It suggests rather than commands. When the basket is full, it does not demand action, it just hints that it might be time.

We referenced butler-type characters like Jarvis from Iron Man as a personality model. Always present, never in the way, and actually useful.

Design System
Designing six motion states

The hardest part of this project was designing the states. We needed six different movements that were distinct enough to tell apart but still felt like they came from the same object. Each one needed a real-world reference so that someone seeing it for the first time could understand it without being told what it meant.

Here is what we landed on:

01
Standby
At rest, but ready
The basket sits still with a very slight rise and fall, like breathing. It is idle but not off. Reference: subtle breathing.
02
Listen
Leaning closer to listen
The basket tilts gently from side to side, like someone leaning in to hear you better. Reference: leaning to hear.
03
Processing
Working on the task
The fabric twists one way then back the other, like cloth being wrung out. The motion stays tight and controlled. Reference: wringing fabric.
04
Acting
Replying enthusiastically
The basket compresses down and bounces back up in a rhythm that matches the pace of speech. Reference: bouncing spring.
05
Reporting
Alerting promptly
The basket deflates slightly then snaps upright, taller and more open. It is more deliberate than the acting state. Reference: stretched fabric.
06
Failure
Something went wrong
The basket slowly collapses flat, stage by stage, then reinflates at the same pace to recover. Reference: collapsed bag.

Concept Validation
Checking if the states made sense

We were not testing the VUI itself since there was no working prototype at this stage. What we wanted to know was whether someone unfamiliar with the project could look at the sketches and understand what each state was trying to say.

We showed the sketches to two people and asked them to describe what they saw without any explanation upfront.

Participant 1
Understood most states without explanation. The listening and acting states were especially clear. The processing state confused them a bit as it looked more like the basket was struggling rather than thinking, though they said it could work if the drawing was not too tight.
Participant 2
Read the upright basket as waiting right away, and the collapsed one as failure. The reporting state felt like the basket was showing or presenting something, which matched what we intended. They noted that some of the calmer states could be more distinct from each other.

The main takeaway was that the basket form works because shape changes are easy to read. The states that had the most physical difference between them were the clearest. The processing state was the main one that needed more work.

We kept the "wringing of fabric" for processing because it still communicates effort, which is accurate. But we would loosened the motion so it does not look like distress.
Reflection
What we would do differently

The biggest lesson from this project is that motion design for VUI is harder than it looks. The states need to be different enough to tell apart at a glance, but they also need to feel like they belong to the same object and personality. We got most of the way there but the calmer states, standby and listen especially, still blur together a bit.

We also relied a lot on the shape of the basket itself to carry the communication. Adding the Snap Device with light and haptics in a real prototype would give us another layer to work with and likely make the states even clearer.

Future Work
Building the conversation

The next step would be building the actual dialogue system that powers Tidylio. Having worked with Voiceflow before to build chatbot flows for companies, the plan would be to map each of the six states to voice intents, responses, and transitions and prototype the full conversation a user would have with the assistant.

Voiceflow Prototype

Design the full conversation flow in Voiceflow: what Tidylio says, when it says it, and how the dialogue moves between states. Then test whether the conversation feels natural and consistent with the personality we designed.

This would also be the first chance to do real usability testing on the VUI rather than just the motion states, which would help close the gap between the design concept and a working experience.
